review_type: Focused narrative review, not a systematic review or exhaustive search
selection: Additional papers absent from the previous 20-entry bibliography. Open primary full texts on IDS explanation comparisons, security evaluation, and explanation evaluation. Dataset records and abstract-only leads do not count.
reading_scope: Targeted reading of methods, evaluation/results and discussion in the available full texts; not a claim of line-by-line reading of every page or independent reproduction of their experiments.

papers.title: Evaluating Explainable AI for Deep Learning-based Network Intrusion Detection System Alert Classification
papers.authors: R. Kalakoti, R. Vaarandi, H. Bahsi, S. Nomm
papers.finding: Real SOC alert prioritization differs from traffic attack classification. DeepLIFT leads several metrics, while LIME's reported faithfulness exceeds SHAP's. Expert-feature alignment is a separate endpoint.
papers.decision: Compare the actual tasks and SHAP variants. Do not present our TreeSHAP deletion finding as universal superiority or human validation.

papers.title: Evaluating The Explainability of State-of-the-Art Machine Learning-based IoT Network Intrusion Detection Systems
papers.authors: A. Kumar and V. L. L. Thing
papers.read: Sections IV-VI; online NIDS case studies and disagreement discussion
papers.finding: TRUSTEE and SHAP can disagree for online IoT detectors; explanation quality and inductive bias vary with architecture.
papers.decision: Distinguish local ranking from global surrogate fidelity. Add a direct discussion of testbed shortcuts and limits of cross-method agreement.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Forensic Analysis: A Comparative Study of SHAP and LIME in Intrusion Detection Models
papers.authors: P. Hermosilla, S. Berrios, and H. Allende-Cid
papers.access: Full PDF accessed through the web reader; local download failed certificate validation and is not claimed as acquired
papers.finding: UNSW-NB15 XGBoost/TabNet comparison includes fidelity, stability and feature-set Jaccard. KernelExplainer uses a 100-record training background; LIME uses 5000 perturbations. Validation and test detector accuracies differ materially.
papers.decision: Acknowledge this close comparison; distinguish KernelSHAP from TreeSHAP and avoid comparing incompatible numerical fidelity scores.

papers.title: A versatile XAI-based framework for efficient and explainable intrusion detection systems
papers.authors: B. Nugraha, A. V. Jnanashree, and T. Bauschert
papers.access: Publisher full HTML read; local PDF request timed out
papers.finding: ANOVA/SHAP feature selection and retraining reduce explanation cost on DDoS/IoT/5G traces. SHAP-LIME consistency and timing are already studied. LIME timing uses 5000 perturbations.
papers.decision: Remove any implied novelty for dual explanations, feature reduction or timing. Qualify budget and hardware dependence; overlap is not explanation ground truth.

papers.title: L-XAIDS: A LIME-based eXplainable AI framework for Intrusion Detection Systems
papers.authors: A. E. Muhammad, K.-C. Yow, N. Bacanin-Dzakula, and M. A. Khan
papers.status: arXiv:2508.17244v1, preprint version reviewed; a Springer journal record also exists
papers.finding: LIME/ELI5 local/global explanations and decision-tree visualizations are established IDS combinations. The reviewed text also discusses CSE-CIC-IDS2018 and LITNET-2020 beyond its main UNSW example.
papers.decision: Do not describe prior work as visualization-only without qualification, or claim that adding LIME makes this framework new.

papers.title: Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning in Computer Security
papers.authors: D. Arp et al.
papers.read: Section 2 pitfalls, empirical impact analysis, Section 7
papers.finding: Sampling, labels, data snooping, spurious correlations, inadequate baselines, base rates and lab-only evaluations can inflate security conclusions.
papers.decision: Add exact feature-pattern exclusion sensitivity, preserve simple baselines, explain class-cap prevalence distortion and refuse deployment claims.

papers.title: TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification across Space and Time
papers.authors: F. Pendlebury, F. Pierazzi, R. Jordaney, J. Kinder, and L. Cavallaro
papers.read: Temporal/spatial constraints C1-C3; Section 4.2; evaluation and supplementary dataset composition
papers.finding: Time ordering and realistic test prevalence change malware evaluation. Random splits and future information can distort measured performance.
papers.decision: State that model seeds reuse one split and do not constitute temporal generalization. Do not transfer malware-specific effect sizes to network data.

papers.title: Troubleshooting an Intrusion Detection Dataset: the CICIDS2017 Case Study
papers.authors: G. Engelen, V. Rimmer, and W. Joosen
papers.status: IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops, pp. 7-12; doi:10.1109/SPW53761.2021.00009
papers.read: Flow/label reconstruction, Section IV-B Table II, Section V
papers.finding: Fixing traffic construction, feature extraction and labels changes class-specific results despite similar aggregate accuracy.
papers.decision: Keep source-to-cohort records and unsupported-label reporting central; explicitly discuss zero Mirai C&C recall rather than only aggregate F1.

papers.title: Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods
papers.authors: D. Slack, S. Hilgard, E. Jia, S. Singh, and H. Lakkaraju
papers.finding: A classifier can treat synthetic perturbations differently from real inputs and conceal discriminatory behavior from perturbation-based explanations.
papers.decision: Describe synthetic masking as an explicit measurement intervention. Do not imply this attack was tested here or that every TreeSHAP implementation has the same vulnerability.

papers.title: The Out-of-Distribution Problem in Explainability and Search Methods for Feature Importance Explanations
papers.authors: P. Hase, H. Xie, and M. Bansal
papers.read: Sections 4-6; replacement functions and counterfactual training
papers.finding: Feature replacement and model behavior outside training support affect deletion-style scores; language-model experiments compare five replacement functions.
papers.decision: Make masking dependence a named construct-validity limitation. The current mask-reference audit is descriptive, not proof of on-manifold validity.

papers.title: A Consistent and Efficient Evaluation Strategy for Attribution Methods
papers.authors: Y. Rong, T. Leemann, V. Borisov, G. Kasneci, and E. Kasneci
papers.finding: Fixed-value image masks can reveal information through removal patterns. ROAD uses noisy linear imputation to improve consistency between removal orders.
papers.decision: Discuss removal-mechanism confounding. Do not insert image-specific ROAD interpolation into mixed categorical network features without validating it.

papers.title: OpenXAI: Towards a Transparent Evaluation of Post hoc Model Explanations
papers.authors: C. Agarwal et al.
papers.read: Sections 1-3; synthetic-data ground truth and metric families
papers.finding: A benchmark can evaluate faithfulness, stability and fairness separately. Data-generating importance is not automatically the fitted model's importance.
papers.decision: Keep model-faithfulness findings distinct from causal attack relevance; do not claim fairness evaluation or explanation ground truth.

papers.title: Quantus: An Explainable AI Toolkit for Responsible Evaluation of Neural Network Explanations and Beyond
papers.authors: A. Hedstrom et al.
papers.finding: Evaluation has several distinct dimensions and depends on metric parameterization, including the feature-replacement baseline.
papers.decision: Separate deletion, repeatability, neighborhood similarity and latency instead of a single unvalidated quality score.

papers.title: The Many Shapley Values for Model Explanation
papers.authors: M. Sundararajan and A. Najmi
papers.finding: Different value functions and baselines yield different Shapley explanations; uniqueness for a specified game does not imply a universal explanation.
papers.decision: Avoid calling SHAP uniquely correct. State attribution output domains and use a common prediction-probability evaluation scale.

papers.title: Explaining individual predictions when features are dependent: More accurate approximations to Shapley values
papers.authors: K. Aas, M. Jullum, and A. Loland
papers.finding: Ignoring dependence can produce unrealistic feature combinations and different attributions; conditional approximations help in the evaluated settings.
papers.decision: Explicitly acknowledge correlated predictors and baseline-dependent conclusions; do not claim a conditional SHAP implementation was run.

papers.title: A Benchmark for Interpretability Methods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: S. Hooker, D. Erhan, P.-J. Kindermans, and B. Kim
papers.read: ROAR definition, redundancy example, Section 4 and conclusion
papers.finding: Retraining after removal addresses a different question from a fixed-model deletion test. Some image attribution estimators do not exceed random importance under ROAR.
papers.decision: Distinguish our primary fixed-model probability drop from training-feature ablation and prior retraining-based evaluation.

papers.title: The Disagreement Problem in Explainable Machine Learning: A Practitioner's Perspective
papers.authors: S. Krishna, T. Han, A. Gu, J. Pombra, S. Jabbari, S. Wu, and H. Lakkaraju
papers.finding: Top-feature overlap, order and contribution signs capture different kinds of disagreement; practitioners' resolution heuristics are not explanation validation.
papers.decision: State that top-5 overlap cannot establish fidelity and do not equate absolute-magnitude deletion with signed explanation agreement.

papers.title: On the Robustness of Interpretability Methods
papers.authors: D. Alvarez-Melis and T. S. Jaakkola
papers.read: Local Lipschitz robustness definition, experiments and Section 4
papers.finding: Small input changes can cause large explanation changes, even when model predictions barely change. Repeated random sampling is a different stability question.
papers.decision: Do not call repeated LIME runs or observational neighborhood cosine an adversarial-robustness test.

papers.title: Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead
papers.authors: C. Rudin
papers.status: Nature Machine Intelligence 1, pp. 206-215; doi:10.1038/s42256-019-0048-x; author preprint reviewed
papers.finding: Accuracy need not require an opaque model; a post-hoc surrogate may omit behavior that matters in high-stakes use.
papers.decision: Retain the depth-5 tree baseline and acknowledge the limited practical motivation for a complex detector when a simple one nearly matches it.

papers.title: Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
papers.authors: M. T. Ribeiro, S. Singh, and C. Guestrin
papers.read: Precision/coverage formulation, user study, realistic perturbation distribution discussion
papers.finding: Rule precision and coverage are explicit and distinct; human simulation performance requires a participant evaluation. Realistic perturbation distributions remain a challenge.
papers.decision: Do not add Anchors solely to increase explainer count. Keep explanation coverage, classification coverage and analyst usefulness distinct.

abstract_only_leads_not_counted.title: A Comparative Evaluation of Shap and Lime for Explainable Machine Learning-Based Intrusion Detection
abstract_only_leads_not_counted.reason: Very recent November 2026 IEEE indexing; abstract available, full text not obtained. Excluded from the 20 full-text reviews and from detailed methodological claims.
